items.stem: Should the federal government make sure every American has health insurance?
items.scope: This is about the goal. How the system works is asked separately.
options: Yes, through one government plan for everyone
Yes, through whatever mix of public and private coverage works
No, but it should help people with low incomes or serious health conditions get covered
No; health coverage is each person's own responsibility

items.stem: Who should be able to get Medicare, the federal health plan now mainly for people 65 and older?
items.scope: Assume people who join would pay premiums or taxes in some form.
options: Everyone, of any age, automatically
Anyone of any age who chooses to buy into it
People 60 and older
Keep it at 65 and older
Raise the age gradually to 67

items.stem: Suppose the US had a government health plan open to everyone. What role should private health insurance have?
items.scope: Answer even if you oppose such a plan.
options: Only cover extras the government plan doesn't, like private rooms
Compete with the government plan; people choose either one
Stay the main system; the government plan is only for people who can't get private coverage

items.stem: What role should the government have in setting prescription drug prices?
items.scope: Think about brand-name drugs with no cheaper generic.
items.context: Medicare now negotiates prices for a limited number of high-cost drugs. The first negotiated prices took effect in January 2026.
options: Set prices for all brand-name drugs, for everyone
Negotiate prices for many more drugs, for both Medicare and private insurance
Negotiate for a limited number of drugs in Medicare, as today
End government price negotiation; let competition set prices

facts.claim: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program: first 10 negotiated prices effective January 1, 2026

items.stem: Should people in the US be able to buy prescription drugs imported from countries where they cost less, such as Canada?
items.scope: Drugs approved in the other country, sold through licensed pharmacies.
options: Yes, from any country with safety standards like ours
Only through limited state programs approved by the FDA
No; imported drugs are too hard to keep safe
items.notes: Cross-cutting candidate; may not load on SOCINS.

items.stem: Which comes closest to what should happen to Medicaid, the health program for people with low incomes?
items.scope: Medicaid is paid for jointly by the federal government and states.
options: Cover all low-income adults in every state, with federal money paying most of the cost
Keep it as is: states choose whether to cover all low-income adults
Limit federal money per person and give states more control over who is covered
Give each state a fixed amount and let it decide everything

definitions.text: A health coverage program for people with low incomes, run by states under federal rules and paid for by both.

items.stem: Should adults on Medicaid who are able to work be required to work, volunteer or go to school to keep their coverage?
items.scope: Think of adults without disabilities or young children.
items.context: A 2025 federal law requires many such adults to do about 80 hours a month of these activities, starting by 2027.
options: No; health coverage shouldn't depend on work
Yes, about 80 hours a month, with exemptions for parents, caregivers and people in school
Yes, with more hours or fewer exemptions than that

facts.claim: Public Law 119-21 requires expansion adults 19-64 to show 80 hours/month of work, community service, or school, with exemptions; states must implement by Jan 1, 2027

items.stem: How should Social Security's funding gap be closed?
items.scope: If nothing changes, benefits would be cut automatically when the trust fund runs out.
items.context: Its trust funds are projected to run out between 2032 and 2034. After that, incoming taxes would pay about 80% of promised benefits.
options: Only raise taxes, mainly on high earners, and keep or increase benefits
Mostly raise taxes, with small benefit changes
An even mix of tax increases and benefit cuts
Mostly slow the growth of benefits, such as by raising the retirement age, with small tax increases
Only slow the growth of benefits; no tax increases

facts.claim: 2026 Trustees Report: OASI reserves depleted in Q4 2032; combined OASDI in Q3 2034, when about 83% of scheduled benefits would be payable
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF13256, 'Social Security: Selected Findings of the 2026 Annual Report' (June 2026)

items.stem: What should Social Security's full retirement age be for people now under 50?
items.scope: Full retirement age is when someone can get their full benefit. Early, reduced benefits could still start at 62.
items.context: Today it is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.
options: Lower it to 65
Keep it at 67
Raise it to 68 or 69
Raise it to 70 or higher

facts.claim: Full retirement age is 67 for people born 1960 or later

items.stem: Should Social Security tax apply to wages above the current limit?
items.scope: The tax is 12.4% of wages, split between worker and employer.
items.context: Today the tax applies only to the first $184,500 a person earns in a year (2026).
options: Yes, on all wages, with no limit
Yes, on wages above $400,000, leaving wages in between untaxed
Raise the limit somewhat, but keep one
Keep the limit as it is
Lower the Social Security tax rate, even if future benefits must shrink

facts.claim: Social Security contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for 2026
facts.source: Social Security Administration, 2026 COLA fact sheet

items.stem: Which comes closest to how Medicare should work for future retirees?
items.scope: Think of people who retire 15 or more years from now.
options: Expand it to cover dental, vision and hearing, paid for with higher taxes
Keep it as it is, adding taxes or savings to pay for it
Give retirees a set amount to choose between traditional Medicare and private plans
Gradually replace it with personal health savings accounts

items.stem: Should retirees with higher incomes pay more for Medicare than others?
items.scope: Higher-income retirees already pay somewhat higher premiums today.
options: Yes, much more than today
Somewhat more than today
Keep it as today
No; everyone paid in and should pay the same
items.notes: Direction relative to G unclear; means-testing appeals to some on both sides. Keep only if it loads.

items.stem: Should workers be able to put part of their Social Security taxes into personal investment accounts?
items.scope: Accounts the worker would own and could invest, for example in stock funds.
options: No; Social Security should remain a guaranteed benefit
Only as an extra on top of Social Security, not taken out of it
Yes, workers could choose to put part of their tax into an account
Yes, and gradually replace Social Security with personal accounts

items.stem: Should people be required to have health insurance?
items.scope: Assume help paying is available for people who can't afford it.
items.context: From 2014 to 2018 there was a federal penalty for having no coverage. The penalty is now $0.
options: Yes, with a penalty for not having it
No penalty, but anyone without insurance is signed up automatically for a free basic plan
No; whether to buy insurance is a personal choice

facts.claim: Individual mandate penalty reduced to $0 starting 2019
facts.source: Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, Public Law 115-97, sec. 11081

items.stem: Should health insurers be allowed to charge more or refuse coverage because of a person's past health problems?
items.scope: Think of conditions like diabetes or cancer that a person had before buying insurance.
items.context: Since 2014 federal law has banned both.
options: No, never, as today
They can charge somewhat more, but not refuse coverage
Yes, with a separate government-funded plan for people insurers turn down

facts.claim: Affordable Care Act bars denial of coverage and premium rating based on health status from 2014

items.stem: Should children have to be vaccinated against diseases like measles and polio to attend school?
items.scope: Think of children with no medical reason to skip. You'll be asked about other exemptions next.
options: Required for both public and private schools
Required for public schools only
Recommended, but parents decide

items.stem: Under the rule you picked, should these children be allowed to skip the required vaccines?
items.scope: Answer each case separately.
options: Should not be allowed to skip
Should be allowed to skip

cases.text: Children whose parents have religious objections
Children whose parents have personal or philosophical objections

items.stem: During a serious outbreak of a contagious disease, should government require most workers to be vaccinated?
items.scope: Assume a vaccine widely judged safe and effective. Medical exemptions always apply.
options: Yes, most workers
Only health care and other close-contact jobs
No government requirement

items.stem: During a serious outbreak, should employers be allowed to require their own workers to be vaccinated?
items.scope: Assume a vaccine widely judged safe and effective. Medical exemptions always apply.
options: Yes, any employer
Only health care employers
No employer

items.subtopic: Immigrants' eligibility for public health benefits
items.stem: Which immigrants should be able to get Medicaid if their incomes are low enough?
items.scope: Emergency room care is always available to everyone and is not part of this question.
items.context: Today most green card holders must wait 5 years. People without legal status are not eligible.
options: Everyone living here, whatever their legal status
Legal immigrants right away, plus children whatever their status
Most legal immigrants after 5 years, as today
Legal immigrants only after 10 years or more
Citizens only

facts.claim: Most lawful permanent residents face a 5-year bar before federal Medicaid eligibility; unauthorized immigrants are eligible only for emergency Medicaid
facts.source: Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996; KFF
facts.note: Public Law 119-21 (2025) narrows Medicaid eligibility for some lawfully present immigrants from late 2026; confirm and adjust context.

items.stem: Should cities add fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay?
items.scope: Most US public water systems do this today.
options: Yes, as health agencies recommend
Let each city decide
No; it should be banned
items.notes: New cross-party coalition since 2024; tests ESTAB and LIBERTY apart from left-right.

items.stem: Should the government ban food additives, such as some artificial dyes, that are allowed in the US but banned in other countries?
items.scope: Additives approved by US regulators.
options: Yes, ban them
Require clear warning labels instead
No; trust US regulators' approval

items.stem: Who should pay for nursing home and home care for older people who can no longer care for themselves?
items.scope: Today Medicare covers little long-term care; Medicaid pays after people spend down their savings.
options: A new government insurance program for everyone
Government help for middle-income families too, not only the poor
Keep today's system
Families and private insurance, with less government help
